passage:
I'm Chetan. Last Thursday I sent the wrong file to a client, and they noticed within the hour. That evening my chest was tight and the usual voice started: careless, idiot, again.
Then I tried something. I imagined Hemant, my flatmate, coming home with the same mistake. He would be gutted. What would I say to him? "You mixed up the folders because you were doing three things at once. You've checked twice on other days. Let's write down the one check that would catch it next time."
So I said that, quietly, to myself. Name the error, name the effort. It felt a bit soppy, and it did help. The next morning I added a folder check to my list and sent the client a plain apology. The mistake was still mine, but it had a next step.

qa.q: Who did Chetan imagine coming home with the same mistake?
qa.a: Chetan imagined Hemant, a flatmate, coming home with the same mistake.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when the usual voice started in the evening?
qa.a: Chetan felt tense and self-critical, with a tight chest and words like careless and idiot.

qa.q: What did Chetan do differently the next morning?
qa.a: Chetan added a folder check to the list and sent the client a plain apology, taking a concrete step instead of only criticising.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel if Chetan spoke to Hemant the way the voice in Chetan's head had spoken?
qa.a: Hemant would probably feel worse and discouraged. That is why Chetan chose to speak kindly, as Chetan would to Hemant.

grounding: A person speaks to themselves after failure as to a friend, naming the error and the effort; self-compassion supports change better than self-contempt.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Simran, accounts.
On Wednesday Simran invoiced the wrong client and only noticed after it was sent. At her desk she said something quietly to herself, and I was close enough to hear. I expected "I'm hopeless." Instead: "Okay. I mixed up two client names. That's the mistake. I checked the amounts carefully, and those are right. What would I say to a colleague? Fix it, then add a name check."
She corrected the invoice, phoned the client herself and put a name check on her list. I said only, "Thanks for telling me." Her voice was steady though her hands were not.
I did not step in. I'll check the next few invoices with her, and I've asked whether she wants a short review on Friday.
— Sarita

qa.q: Which client detail did Simran mix up?
qa.a: Simran mixed up two client names.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling after she noticed the invoice mistake?
qa.a: Simran was upset and shaken, since her hands were not steady, but she spoke to herself calmly and stayed focused on fixing it.

qa.q: What did Simran do after speaking to herself that turned the mistake into a step forward?
qa.a: Simran corrected the invoice, phoned the client herself and put a name check on her list.

qa.q: How did Sarita respond, and what might Sarita have been thinking?
qa.a: Sarita said only thanks for telling me, and did not step in. Sarita seems to have seen that Simran was handling it and offered support without taking over.

grounding: A person speaks to herself after failure as she would to a colleague, naming the error and the effort, which supports change.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Missed the quarterly report deadline today. My manager had to explain it to the client, and she looked tired, not angry, which was worse.
On the bus home I heard the old voice: "You're hopeless. You always do this." Then I tried the thing the counsellor suggested. If Jaya had missed this deadline, what would I tell her?
I'd say: "You made an error. You took on the vendor audit and the report in the same week, and you didn't flag it early. That's the mistake. But you also stayed late every day and checked every number twice. That counts."
So I wrote it down, to me. It felt silly. Then it helped. Tomorrow I'll tell my manager I should have flagged the clash on Friday, and I'll suggest a check-in rule for weeks like this.
Pradeep

qa.q: What deadline did Pradeep miss?
qa.a: The quarterly report deadline.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: Pradeep felt ashamed and self-critical at first, hearing the voice call him hopeless, before trying a kinder approach.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's kinder note do better than 'You're hopeless'?
qa.a: It names the real error and the effort, which leads to a clear fix like flagging clashes early instead of just self-blame.

qa.q: How might the manager see Pradeep's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: The manager would probably feel reassured and respect Pradeep more for owning the error and suggesting a fix.

grounding: Shows a person speaking to themselves after a failure as they would to a friend, naming the error and the effort, which leads to better change.

passage:
Ankita: failed the driving test. third time
Ankita: I'm literally the most useless person alive
Kashish: oh no 😔 what happened?
Ankita: stalled on the slope. then panicked at the roundabout
Kashish: ok. question. if I failed a third time and texted you "I'm useless", what would you say to me?
Ankita: ...I'd say you're not useless, you're nervous
Kashish: go on
Ankita: I'd say the slope is hard and you got further than last time. last time you stalled at the gate
Kashish: so?
Ankita: so I got further. and the actual error is the handbrake on slopes
Kashish: that's the most useful thing you've said all evening 🙂
Ankita: lol. ok. booking two slope lessons with the instructor this week
Ankita: still sad though
Kashish: allowed. both things can be true

qa.q: Where did Ankita stall during the test?
qa.a: Ankita stalled on the slope.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling right after failing the test?
qa.a: Ankita felt frustrated and ashamed, typing 'the most useless person alive'.

qa.q: How did Kashish's question change Ankita's thinking?
qa.a: By asking what Ankita would say to a friend, it helped Ankita name the real error and the progress made, which led to booking slope lessons.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel seeing Ankita's plan?
qa.a: Kashish is probably pleased and relieved that the self-contempt turned into something useful.

grounding: Shows a person speaking to themselves after failure as they would to a friend, naming the error and the effort, leading to a practical change.

passage: Lokesh walked home along the canal path from the village school in Sirsa, dust on his shoes and a knot in his stomach. The district inspector had watched his science lesson that morning, and it had gone badly. The seed experiment didn't sprout, two boys fought, and he lost track of time. "Idiot," he muttered at the sugarcane. Then he stopped. His sister Lakshmi had failed her first lesson inspection last year, and he'd sat with her on the roof and said all the right things. He tried saying them to himself, out loud, feeling a bit foolish. "Okay. The seeds were planted too late. That's the error. The fight, you handled calmly. You're three months into the job and you care about these kids." By the time he reached the gate, the knot had loosened. He wrote "plant seeds a week earlier" in his notebook.

qa.q: What went wrong with the seed experiment?
qa.a: The seeds didn't sprout because they were planted too late.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on the walk home at first?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and tense, with a knot in his stomach, calling himself an idiot.

qa.q: What did talking to himself as he talked to Lakshmi make possible?
qa.a: It helped him name the real error and his effort, so he left with a practical fix: plant seeds a week earlier.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi react if she heard what he told himself?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and proud that the words he once gave her were now helping him.

grounding: Shows a young teacher speaking to himself after a failed lesson as he would to his sister, naming the error and the effort.

passage: On the bus home through Lagos traffic, Ada replayed the meeting: the load figure she had copied wrong, her manager's frown, the redo that cost the team two days. Her first thought was the usual one. Stupid. Careless. You'll never be good at this. Then she remembered what she had told Abebe last month when he failed his licensing exam: "You studied every night for months. You got one section wrong. Find out which and fix it." She took out her notebook and wrote to herself the way she had talked to him. "Ada, you copied one number wrong. You were rushing because you stayed late helping on the other file. Next time: check the figures before sending." She read it twice. Her shoulders came down from her ears. Tomorrow she would ask her manager for a second check on big numbers.

qa.q: What mistake did Ada make at work?
qa.a: She copied a load figure wrong.

qa.q: How did Ada feel after writing to herself the way she had talked to Abebe?
qa.a: She felt calmer and relieved; her shoulders came down from her ears.

qa.q: What made Ada's note to herself useful and not just kind?
qa.a: It named the exact error, why she was rushing and one fix to try, so it pointed toward change rather than only comfort.

qa.q: What would change if Ada kept calling herself stupid?
qa.a: She would probably feel worse and more afraid of mistakes, and be less likely to ask for the second check that could prevent the next one.

grounding: Shows a young adult after a work mistake speaking to herself as she would to a friend, naming both the error and the effort.
